findings.reason: Pre-approval is the lender's maximum, not a budget (CFPB), and the full monthly cost includes taxes, insurance, HOA fees and repairs (CFPB). Changed 'free' to 'little or no cost': CFPB and HUD materials say 'free or low-cost' / 'often at little or no cost', not free. Down-payment help via HUD-approved counselors is CFPB's own advice.

sources.quote: A lender's preapproval represents the maximum that they are willing to lend to you. This is not a financial directive—you can always spend less.
Focus on a mortgage that is affordable for you given your other priorities, not how much you qualify for. Lenders will often tell you how much you are qualified to borrow

Homeowner's insurance, property taxes, and possibly private mortgage insurance or homeowners association fees are typically added to your monthly mortgage payment ... There may also be costs for repairs and maintenance of your home.
The counseling agencies on the searchable list are approved by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) and they can offer independent advice, often at little or no cost to you.
The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) sponsors housing counseling agencies throughout the country to provide free or low-cost advice.

Many states and local organizations offer programs to help first-time buyers with a down payment or closing costs. To find programs near you, look up a HUD-approved housing counseling agency in your area.

findings.reason: Needs a new 'First year' step (homestead exemption application and how the deed is titled), which changes the playbook's shape. 'Often lasts the life of the loan' replaced with HUD's actual rule for FHA case numbers assigned on or after June 3, 2013 (more than 90% LTV: the loan term, up to 30 years; 90% or less: up to 11 years). 'Closing papers say which you have' made specific: the Closing Disclosure's 'Loan Type' field (Reg. Z). Checker: automatic termination wording follows 12 U.S.C. 4902(b)(1)-(2) (on the termination date if current, otherwise once current).

blocks.body: On a conventional loan, the lender must drop PMI automatically when the balance is scheduled to reach 78% of the original value and you are current on payments, and you can request removal at 80%. Note the date. FHA mortgage insurance follows HUD's rules instead: on FHA loans started after mid-2013, the annual premium lasts the whole loan term (up to 30 years) if you borrowed more than 90% of the home's value, and up to 11 years otherwise. Your Closing Disclosure names the loan type.
blocks.plain: With a conventional loan, the lender must drop private mortgage insurance on its own once your balance is scheduled to reach 78% of the home's original value and you are up to date on payments. You can ask for it to be removed at 80%. Write down the date. FHA loans follow HUD's rules instead. On FHA loans started after mid-2013, if you borrowed more than 90% of the home's value, the yearly premium lasts for the whole loan (up to 30 years). If you borrowed 90% or less, it lasts up to 11 years. Your Closing Disclosure shows which loan type you have.

blocks.notes: Lean = the full proposal's pmi text unchanged; nothing in it could be cut without leaving ADV-26 (HIGH) half-fixed. 'and you are current on payments' is the HIGH fix's own condition (12 U.S.C. 4902(b)). The FHA sentence with HUD's durations is what replaces the reviewer's 'often lasts the life of the loan' (the full proposal corrected that wording from HUD's rule), and it is what stops an FHA borrower waiting for a drop-off; cutting the durations would leave 'follows HUD's rules instead' with no content, and any shorter paraphrase ('can last much longer') would be a new claim. 'Your Closing Disclosure names the loan type' is the reviewer's 'your closing papers say which you have', made specific. CFP-27 (LOW) is covered as a side effect: the same sentences are its fix, nothing extra was added for it. Numbers {78%, 80%, 2013, 30, 90%, 11} identical in body and plain.

owner_decisions.what: Add a 'First year' step to the home-purchase playbook: apply for any property-tax homestead exemption by the local deadline, and confirm how the deed is titled.
owner_decisions.why_owner: It adds a new step to the playbook (changes the product's shape), and both points are state law with no federal primary source, so the wording has to stay hedged and its audit rows cannot reach PASS without a decision on which state sources to cite or whether to leave it as a 'check your state' pointer.

draft.title: Check the property-tax exemption and how the deed is titled
draft.body: In many states the county or local tax office offers a homestead or owner-occupant property-tax exemption that you have to apply for, often by a deadline, so check with yours. Also confirm how the deed is titled, because the form of ownership affects who owns the home if one owner dies.
draft.plain: In many states, your county or local tax office gives owners who live in their home a lower property tax, but you have to apply, often by a deadline. Check with yours. Also check how your deed names the owners, because that affects who owns the home if one owner dies.
props: Many states offer a homestead/owner-occupant property-tax exemption
You usually have to apply, often by a deadline
Check with the local tax office
Confirm how the deed is titled
how your deed names the owners
Form of ownership affects who owns the home if an owner dies
